q: Which testicular cells contain Reinke crystals?
x: Leydig cells. These interstitial cells are rich in smooth endoplasmic reticulum for steroid synthesis, and rod-shaped Reinke crystals can be found in their cytoplasm, a feature that also marks Leydig cell tumors.

w.Sertoli cells: Sertoli cells sit inside the tubule and answer FSH; they have a pale nucleus with a prominent nucleolus and tight junctions, and they make inhibin B and androgen-binding protein rather than steroid hormones.
w.Spermatogonia: Spermatogonia are germ stem cells on the basement membrane that divide by mitosis; they have no steroid-making machinery and carry no crystalloid inclusions.
w.Peritubular myoid cells: Myoid cells are smooth-muscle-like cells around the tubule that contract to move sperm toward the rete testis, and they are not steroid producers.
w.Primary spermatocytes: Primary spermatocytes are the largest germ cells, with coarse chromatin from a long prophase of meiosis I, and they hold no crystalloids.

pt.say: The interstitium panel lists Reinke crystals beside the Leydig cells, which carry LH receptors and make testosterone, so the crystals belong to Leydig cells.

q: In which compartment of the seminiferous tubule do spermatogonia sit?
x: Basal compartment. Spermatogonia rest on the basement membrane below the Sertoli tight junctions, so they lie outside the blood-testis barrier; committed daughter cells cross the junctions to reach the adluminal compartment for meiosis.

w.Adluminal compartment, inside the barrie: The adluminal compartment lies above the junctions and holds primary and secondary spermatocytes and spermatids, the cells whose antigens the barrier hides from the immune system.
w.Interstitium beside the capillaries: The interstitium lies outside the tubule altogether and holds Leydig cells, capillaries and connective tissue rather than germ cells.
w.Lumen of the tubule: The lumen is where finished but immotile sperm are released and carried toward the rete testis, not where the stem cells reside.
w.Rete testis: The rete testis is the network of channels in the mediastinum that collects sperm from the tubules before the efferent ductules; it holds no germ cell stem cells.

pt.say: The basal compartment label sits beside the spermatogonia on the basement membrane, outside the barrier, while the adluminal compartment above holds the meiotic cells.

q: Which Sertoli cell product keeps testosterone concentrated inside the seminiferous tubule?
x: Androgen-binding protein. Under FSH, Sertoli cells secrete it into the tubule, where it holds testosterone at 50 to 100 times the serum level, the high local concentration that spermatogenesis requires.

w.Inhibin B: Inhibin B travels to the pituitary and suppresses FSH; it signals the state of the tubules rather than binding testosterone locally.
w.Anti-Müllerian hormone: Anti-Müllerian hormone is secreted in the fetus and causes regression of the Müllerian ducts; it does not retain testosterone in the tubule.
w.Sex hormone-binding globulin: Sex hormone-binding globulin is made by the liver and carries testosterone in the blood; it is the circulating counterpart, not the Sertoli product acting within the tubule.
w.Estradiol: Estradiol is a steroid made by aromatase, mostly in fat, that feeds back on the pituitary; it does not bind and hold testosterone.

hl: ABP keeps testosterone 50 to 100 times serum
pt.say: The inside-the-tubule note says ABP keeps testosterone 50 to 100 times serum, so androgen-binding protein is the Sertoli product that concentrates testosterone in the tubule.

q: Which step of spermatogenesis remodels spermatids into spermatozoa without cell division?
x: Spermiogenesis. The Golgi apparatus builds the acrosome, a centriole grows the flagellum, mitochondria wrap the midpiece and Sertoli cells engulf the shed cytoplasm, all without any division of the haploid spermatid.

w.Spermiation: Spermiation is the release of finished sperm into the lumen after remodeling is complete; it frees the cell and does not change its shape.
w.Meiosis I: Meiosis I is a division in which primary spermatocytes separate homologous chromosomes to form secondary spermatocytes, so it does involve cell division.
w.Meiosis II: Meiosis II divides each secondary spermatocyte within hours into two spermatids, so it includes division, whereas the remodeling that follows does not.
w.Spermatocytogenesis: Spermatocytogenesis is the mitotic phase in which spermatogonia divide and give rise to primary spermatocytes, so it relies on cell division.

pt.say: The adluminal compartment lists spermatids undergoing spermiogenesis, the remodeling stage that follows meiosis II and ends with spermatozoa released into the lumen.

q: In what state are sperm when they are released into the tubule lumen?
x: Immotile and unable to fertilize. The testis builds the sperm, the epididymis then gives it forward motility, and capacitation and the acrosome reaction occur only in the female tract.

w.Motile but not yet capacitated: That describes sperm after epididymal transit, where the head and body of the epididymis give them forward motility; sperm leaving the testis have not had this maturation.
w.Fully capacitated: Capacitation occurs in the female reproductive tract after ejaculation, so sperm leaving the testis are far from capacitated.
w.Hyperactivated with the acrosome reacted: Hyperactivated motility and the acrosome reaction occur near the egg in the oviduct, long after sperm have left the testis.
w.Motile and able to fertilize: Sperm leaving the testis need epididymal maturation and female tract capacitation before they can swim forward and fertilize an egg.

pt.say: The lumen labels read released but still immotile, so spermatozoa leave the tubule unable to swim forward and gain motility later in the epididymis.

q: Which binding protein rises with age and makes free testosterone fall faster than total testosterone?
x: SHBG. Liver production of sex hormone-binding globulin increases with age, binding more testosterone tightly, so the free and bioavailable fractions decline faster than the roughly 1 percent a year fall in total testosterone.

w.Albumin: Albumin binds testosterone only loosely and counts toward bioavailable hormone; its level changes little with normal aging, so it does not explain the faster fall in free hormone.
w.Androgen-binding protein: Androgen-binding protein is the Sertoli cell version that holds testosterone inside the tubule; the circulating binder that rises with age is made by the liver.
w.Transcortin: Transcortin, or cortisol-binding globulin, carries cortisol and rises with estrogen, but it has little affinity for testosterone and is not the age-related binder.
w.Thyroxine-binding globulin: Thyroxine-binding globulin carries thyroid hormone rather than androgens, so its level plays no part in the age-related fall of free testosterone.

hl: SHBG rises, so free testosterone falls faster
Testosterone falls about 1% a year after 40
pt.say: The aging panel states that SHBG rises, so free testosterone falls faster than the roughly 1 percent yearly fall in total testosterone after age 40.

q: Which enzyme in fat converts testosterone to estradiol?
x: Aromatase. Fat is the main site of this conversion in men, so obesity raises estradiol and lowers testosterone and LH, while the estradiol it makes closes the epiphyses and maintains bone density.

w.5-alpha-reductase: 5-alpha-reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone in the prostate, skin and hair follicles, a more potent androgen, rather than to an estrogen.
w.Desmolase: Desmolase, the side-chain cleavage enzyme, converts cholesterol to pregnenolone, the first committed step of steroid synthesis, long before testosterone exists.
w.17-alpha-hydroxylase: 17-alpha-hydroxylase acts early in the pathway, steering pregnenolone and progesterone toward androgen precursors and cortisol; it does not act on testosterone itself.
w.Sulfatase: Steroid sulfatase removes sulfate groups, for example converting DHEA sulfate to DHEA; it does not make estradiol from testosterone.

pt.say: The estradiol branch shows aromatase in fat turning testosterone into estradiol, a conversion that rises with obesity and feeds back on LH.

q: How much higher is the testosterone concentration inside the seminiferous tubule than in serum?
x: About 50 to 100 times. Androgen-binding protein keeps testosterone made by Leydig cells concentrated in the tubule, and spermatogenesis needs this gradient; injected testosterone suppresses LH, collapses the local level and stops sperm production.

w.About the same: If tubular and serum levels were equal, spermatogenesis would not depend on LH-driven local production, yet injected testosterone, which raises blood levels, still causes azoospermia.
w.About 2 times: A twofold gradient is far too small to explain why testosterone from injections cannot replace the local concentration that Leydig cells and binding protein provide.
w.About 10 times: Ten times still understates the gradient, which is closer to 50 to 100 times, and that is why high blood testosterone from injections cannot substitute for local production.
w.About 1000 times: A thousandfold gradient overstates the measured difference; intratesticular testosterone is on the order of 50 to 100 times the circulating level.

hl: ABP keeps testosterone 50 to 100 times serum
pt.say: The inside-the-tubule note states that ABP keeps testosterone 50 to 100 times serum, a gradient that LH-driven local production maintains and exogenous testosterone destroys.

q: Which pattern of GnRH secretion keeps LH and FSH release going?
x: Pulses every 1 to 2 hours. The pituitary needs pulsatile GnRH; continuous exposure, as from a long-acting agonist such as leuprolide, downregulates the receptors, shuts off LH and FSH and lowers testosterone.

w.Continuous infusion: Continuous GnRH desensitizes the pituitary and downregulates its receptors, which is why agonists such as leuprolide lower testosterone after an initial flare.
w.One surge each day: Men do not rely on a single daily surge; the pituitary needs repeated pulses through the day, and the morning peak of testosterone is a gentle rhythm layered on top.
w.Release only at night: GnRH pulses continue around the clock in adult men; restricting release to the night would not sustain the steady gonadotropin output that Leydig and Sertoli cells need.
w.Release only during puberty: Adults keep depending on GnRH pulses after puberty; if release stopped, as in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, testosterone and sperm production would fall.

pt.say: The hypothalamus box labels GnRH in pulses, which release LH and FSH from the pituitary; pulsatile release, not continuous exposure, sustains the axis.

q: Which nerves carry the sympathetic fibers that cause emission of semen?
x: Hypogastric nerves. Sympathetic fibers from T10 to L2 contract the ductus deferens, seminal vesicles and prostate and close the bladder neck, moving semen into the urethra before pudendal-driven ejaculation expels it.

w.Pelvic splanchnic nerves: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 that produce erection by nitric oxide release, not the sympathetic squeeze of emission.
w.Pudendal nerve: The pudendal nerve is somatic and drives the rhythmic bulbospongiosus contractions of ejaculation itself, the phase that follows emission.
w.Genitofemoral nerve: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster and the skin of the upper thigh and mediates the cremasteric reflex; it plays no part in emission.
w.Ilioinguinal nerve: The ilioinguinal nerve gives sensation to the anterior scrotum or labia and the upper medial thigh; it carries no autonomic fibers for emission.

pt.say: In the point, squeeze, shoot panel, the squeeze step is emission carried by sympathetic hypogastric nerves, which make the ductus, vesicles and prostate contract.

q: Which nerve drives the rhythmic bulbospongiosus contractions of ejaculation?
x: Pudendal nerve. Somatic fibers from S2 to S4 make the bulbospongiosus and ischiocavernosus contract rhythmically to expel semen, whereas sympathetic damage leaves orgasm with retrograde or absent ejaculate.

w.Hypogastric nerves: Hypogastric nerves are sympathetic and cause emission and bladder neck closure before ejaculation; they do not drive the rhythmic muscular expulsion itself.
w.Pelvic splanchnic nerves: Pelvic splanchnic nerves supply the parasympathetic input for erection through nitric oxide and do not control skeletal muscle contraction.
w.Genitofemoral nerve: The genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremaster muscle and upper thigh skin and has no motor role in the muscles around the penile bulb.
w.Inferior rectal nerve: The inferior rectal nerve is a branch of the pudendal nerve that supplies the external anal sphincter and perianal skin, not the penile muscles.

pt.say: In the shoot step, ejaculation is somatic and carried by the pudendal nerve, which makes the bulbospongiosus contract to expel semen.

q: Which enzyme makes cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle after nitric oxide arrives?
x: Guanylate cyclase. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase, which converts GTP to cGMP; cGMP activates protein kinase G, calcium falls, the smooth muscle relaxes and the sinusoids fill, while PDE5 later breaks cGMP down.

w.Adenylate cyclase: Adenylate cyclase makes cAMP, the messenger used by alprostadil and prostaglandin receptors, a parallel route to erection rather than the nitric oxide pathway.
w.Nitric oxide synthase: Nitric oxide synthase makes nitric oxide in nerves and endothelium upstream; the cGMP is made afterward, by the enzyme that nitric oxide activates.
w.Phosphodiesterase type 5: Phosphodiesterase type 5 destroys cGMP and ends the erection; sildenafil blocks it, so it lowers the messenger rather than making it.
w.Protein kinase G: Protein kinase G is activated by cGMP and lowers calcium in the smooth muscle; it acts downstream of the messenger instead of producing it.

hl: Guanylate cyclase makes cGMP from GTP
pt.say: The second step in the cascade reads guanylate cyclase makes cGMP from GTP, after nitric oxide is released and before protein kinase G lowers calcium.

q: Which gland's secretion supplies the fructose that sperm use for energy?
x: Seminal vesicles. They add an alkaline, fructose-rich fluid that makes up about 65 to 75 percent of semen volume; when obstruction or absent vasa remove it, the ejaculate becomes scant, acidic and fructose-negative.

w.Prostate: The prostate adds PSA, citrate, zinc and acid phosphatase, and PSA liquefies the coagulum; it supplies about 20 to 30 percent of the volume but not the sperm fuel.
w.Bulbourethral glands: The bulbourethral glands release a small amount of clear mucus before ejaculation to lubricate the urethra, and they add little volume.
w.Epididymis: The epididymis absorbs fluid, matures sperm and stores them in its tail; it is a duct, not a gland that adds fructose to semen.
w.Efferent ductules: The efferent ductules reabsorb most of the testicular fluid and so concentrate the sperm; they remove fluid rather than add fructose.

hl: Low volume, acidic pH, no fructose
pt.say: The semen branch of the work-up reads low volume, acidic pH, no fructose, which means seminal vesicle fluid is missing, showing that the seminal vesicles supply the fructose.

q: Which zone of the prostate is felt on rectal examination and gives rise to most cancers?
x: Peripheral zone. It makes up about 70 percent of the gland, lies posteriorly where a finger in the rectum can feel it, and gives rise to 70 to 80 percent of cancers, whereas BPH arises in the transition zone around the urethra.

w.Transition zone: The transition zone surrounds the urethra and is where benign prostatic hyperplasia arises, causing early urinary obstruction; it is not the usual site of cancer or the zone palpable on rectal examination.
w.Central zone: The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely diseased, and it lies deep within the gland rather than against the rectum.
w.Anterior fibromuscular stroma: The anterior fibromuscular stroma is muscle and fibrous tissue without glands, so adenocarcinoma does not arise there.
w.Periurethral glands: Periurethral glands lie in the transition territory around the urethra and belong to the BPH region, not to the posterior zone felt through the rectum.

hl: Posterior: a hard nodule is felt on rectal exam
pt.say: The peripheral zone is posterior and about 70 percent of the gland, so a hard nodule is felt on rectal exam, and it accounts for 70 to 80 percent of cancers.

q: Which venous network cools arterial blood on its way to the testis by countercurrent exchange?
x: Pampiniform plexus. These veins wrap the testicular artery in the spermatic cord, so warm arterial blood hands heat to cooler venous blood before reaching the testis, keeping it 2 to 4 degrees Celsius below core temperature for spermatogenesis.

w.Cremasteric veins: The cremasteric veins drain the cremaster and cord coverings and do not wrap the testicular artery, so they are not the heat exchanger; the cremaster muscle instead adjusts the testis position.
w.Dorsal vein of the penis: The deep dorsal vein of the penis drains the erectile tissue through the subtunical plexus and has no relation to the testicular artery.
w.Prostatic venous plexus: The prostatic venous plexus drains the prostate and connects to the vertebral veins, a route for prostate cancer spread, and it has no role in cooling the testis.
w.Vertebral venous plexus: The vertebral venous plexus communicates with the pelvic veins and can carry prostate cancer cells to the spine; it is not part of the spermatic cord.
